lines.text: Rahul built a placement bot. He asks it to explain binary search, then watches a spinner for six long seconds.
Same bot, same model, with streaming switched on: the first word shows up almost at once.
The model isn't any faster. It writes one token at a time either way, and the last word lands at the same moment.
What changed is the time to first token. That's the clock your users actually feel.
Here's the path. The browser sends one request to your FastAPI backend, which calls the model with stream set to true.
Every chunk that comes back is yielded into a streaming response, so it leaves your server immediately.
On the wire it's Server-Sent Events: a line starting with data, then a blank line. Plain HTTP.
Wrap each token in JSON, because a token can contain a newline, and a raw newline breaks the message.
In the browser, fetch reads the stream. One read can hold three events, or half of one.
So keep a buffer, split on the blank line, and add each token to the page.
After you deploy, test it again. A proxy that buffers will hand over the whole answer in one lump.
So remember: streaming doesn't cut total time or cost. It cuts the wait before the first word.
Next lesson: cost, latency and caching.
